lines.text: Our story begins in Tokyo, in 1908.

shots.on_screen: Tokyo 1908 at dusk, tall vertical composition: sky at top, period wooden two-storey street receding, a lit laboratory window. Respectful, period-plausible, not exoticized.
shots.camera: Descending crane (tilt down) toward the window.
shots.transition_in: Dip from black (0.3 s, internal join)

lines.text: A chemist named Kikunae Ikeda was eating a bowl of soup made with kombu, a kind of seaweed.

shots.on_screen: Professor Ikeda, waist-up, blowing on a steaming bowl. A kombu strip floats up out of the bowl as an icon.

layout.TOP: Name tag KIKUNAE IKEDA; then KOMBU icon+label

lines.text: He noticed a taste that wasn't sweet, or sour, or salty, or bitter. It was something else. Savory. Meaty. Deep.

shots.on_screen: Four taste icons pop around Ikeda's head (2x2 around the head) on each word, each dimming right after.

lines.text: He noticed a taste that wasn't sweet, or sour, or salty, or bitter. It was something else. Savory. Meaty. Deep.

shots.on_screen: A fifth empty slot glows with a pulsing '?'; three words drift up in sequence.

lines.text: So he went to his lab, boiled down huge amounts of seaweed, and found the source: a substance called glutamic acid.

shots.on_screen: Lab: a comically tall pile of seaweed tumbles from the top of frame into a giant pot; it boils.
shots.camera: Tilt down with the falling seaweed.

lines.text: So he went to his lab, boiled down huge amounts of seaweed, and found the source: a substance called glutamic acid.

shots.on_screen: Time-lapse: pile shrinks, steam rises, boils down to a dish with a few glinting crystals.
shots.camera: Tilt down from steam to dish, push-in.

lines.text: He named the taste umami. Roughly: delicious taste.

shots.on_screen: The fifth slot fills: UMAMI pops big; the other four tastes return around it as equals.

lines.text: To turn it into a seasoning, he paired it with sodium, making a stable, salt-like crystal. Monosodium glutamate.

shots.on_screen: Glutamate mascot (first time in the story) meets a small sodium ion character; they click together.

lines.text: To turn it into a seasoning, he paired it with sodium, making a stable, salt-like crystal. Monosodium glutamate.

shots.on_screen: The pair tiles into a growing salt-like crystal; full name appears with M, S, G highlighted.

shots.on_screen: Crystals pour into the MSG shaker (first canonical appearance), which lands on a period shop counter.

lines.text: Here's the thing. Glutamate isn't some strange lab-made chemical.

shots.transition_in: Dip from black (0.3 s, internal join)

scenes.title: What Happens When You Eat It

lines.text: Almost all the MSG you eat never even makes it into your blood. Here's why.

shots.on_screen: HOOK: lit on frame 0. A shaker at the top pours a stream of glutamate mascots down a vertical stylized gut funnel; gut cells lining it gobble almost all of them; only a stray one or two trickle into a thin blood vessel at the bottom. On 'Here's why' the camera snaps toward the mouth/top.

layout.TOP: PART 2/3 · THE SCIENCE tag + keyword WHERE DOES IT GO?
layout.LOW: Thin blood vessel with a 1-2 particle trickle

shots.camera: Slow tilt down with the stream; snap up on 'Here's why'.

shots.hero: Part 2 hook: pouring stream eaten by the gut
shots.notes: Do not show 95% here; the number lands later on the spoken word (s05 counter).

lines.text: So what happens when you eat it?

shots.on_screen: A fork lifts a bite of seasoned food from a plate (LOW) up to a mouth in profile (MID).

lines.text: First, glutamate docks onto special receptors on your tongue, and sends your brain a message: this food has protein in it. Yum.

shots.on_screen: Full-height cutaway body (head at top of MID, torso below). Push into the tongue: receptors as docking cups; mascots dock with a click and glow.

lines.text: First, glutamate docks onto special receptors on your tongue, and sends your brain a message: this food has protein in it. Yum.

shots.on_screen: A signal pulse travels up a nerve to the brain; the brain pops a speech bubble.

lines.text: Then it reaches your gut. And this is where the scary story starts to fall apart.

shots.on_screen: Camera dives down the oesophagus into the gut tunnel. On 'fall apart' a small '!' alarm bubble (s01 keyword style) cracks and crumbles.

lines.text: The cells lining your intestines love glutamate. They burn it as fuel.

shots.on_screen: Intestine wall: round gut-cell characters gobble passing mascots and light up with a small energy spark.

layout.MID: Row of gut cells (2 rows stacked)

lines.text: Almost all the glutamate you eat, around ninety-five percent, is used up right there in your gut, before it ever reaches your bloodstream.

lines.text: Almost all the glutamate you eat, around ninety-five percent, is used up right there in your gut, before it ever reaches your bloodstream.

lines.text: And the little that slips through faces another wall: the blood-brain barrier, a tightly guarded border that controls what gets into your brain.

shots.on_screen: Follow the few particles up a vessel to the head; a castle-wall barrier rises across the frame with cute guards.

lines.text: And the little that slips through faces another wall: the blood-brain barrier, a tightly guarded border that controls what gets into your brain.

lines.text: Scientists took the claims seriously, and tested them. Again, and again.

shots.on_screen: The claims, re-established for this part: keyword cards EXCITOTOXIN?!, POISON!, HEADACHES? (same style as s01 keywords) get pinned to a lab corkboard; a diverse team of scientists below; folders stack and get checks.
shots.transition_in: Dip from black (0.3 s, internal join)
shots.notes: No study count on the folders.

lines.text: The gold standard is a double-blind study: people get either MSG or a placebo, and nobody, not even the researchers, knows who got which.

shots.on_screen: Gold-standard badge, then two identical capsules labeled A and B side by side.

lines.text: The gold standard is a double-blind study: people get either MSG or a placebo, and nobody, not even the researchers, knows who got which.

shots.on_screen: Capsules drop under two cups and shuffle; volunteer and researcher both wear cute blindfolds.

lines.text: Over and over, people who said they were sensitive to MSG reacted just as often to the fake.

lines.text: Over and over, people who said they were sensitive to MSG reacted just as often to the fake.

lines.text: Huge doses on an empty stomach caused mild, short-lived symptoms in some people. But the results weren't consistent, and nothing like that showed up with normal amounts in normal food.

continuity.rules: One prop (placeholder KZ.shaker(...,'MSG')); label reads exactly 'MSG'. Negative contexts change overlays/lighting (X, reticle), never the prop.

continuity.name: Salt shaker
continuity.rules: Same silhouette as MSG shaker, different body/cap tone; label 'SALT'.

continuity.name: Retro TV wall
continuity.rules: 3x3 grid ~860 px wide centered on x=490 in MID (background rows may continue into UI zones). Slots: HOST=B2 (center), TVDOC=A1, CHEF=C1, GURU=A3, AUNT=C3; other 4 = static. Light-up order s01: B2,A1,C1,A3,C3; switch-off order s09: C3,A3,C1,A1,B2. Silhouettes with role props; no real likeness; invented channel names only.

continuity.rules: Whenever a talking head is visible: 'DRAMATIZATION - fictional character' in the role lower-third (LOW zone) and a DRAMATIZATION pill in TOP; text >= 40 px.

continuity.name: Chapter labels
continuity.rules: Same chapter-label component (placeholder KZ.chapter), placed in TOP zone, left-aligned at x=40.

continuity.name: PART n/3 tag
continuity.rules: Pill in TOP zone, left-aligned x=40, y~230-290: 'PART n/3 · <PART TITLE>'. Pops in within 0.3 s of a part opener, stays large ~3 s, then shrinks to a small persistent pill for the rest of the opening scene.

continuity.name: End card
continuity.rules: One component for all three parts: 'PART n →' + part title (parts 1-2), series title + 'PART 3/3' (part 3). Sits in MID/LOW above the caption band; lands on the spoken word 'part'; holds to the last frame.

allowed_numbers_and_claims: '50+ YEARS' / 'more than fifty years' (s01); '50 YEARS OF FEAR' (s06 hook: 'Fifty years of fear')
1908, Tokyo, Kikunae Ikeda, kombu, glutamic acid, umami ~ 'delicious taste', sodium + glutamate = monosodium glutamate, on sale 'within a year' (s03) - NO year for the sale
Glutamate: one of the most common amino acids; protein building block; tomatoes, mushrooms, soy sauce, parmesan ('one of the richest') (s04)
Human breast milk ~10x more FREE glutamate than cow's milk (s04): '~10x', bars ~10:1
Body makes its own glutamate every day; tomato glutamate = MSG glutamate (s04)
Almost all MSG you eat never makes it into the blood (s05 hook); ~95% used in the gut (s05) - the ONLY percentage; never '5%'
1968 letter to the New England Journal of Medicine; numbness, weakness, palpitations; suspects wine, salt, MSG; 'a guess'; headline 'Chinese Restaurant Syndrome' (s06)
1969: huge doses injected under the skin of newborn mice, brain damage found (s06) - no gore

Double-blind placebo testing; sensitive people reacted as often to placebo; huge doses on an empty stomach -> mild, short-lived symptoms in some, inconsistent; nothing with normal amounts in normal food (s07)
US FDA 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS), same category as salt, sugar, baking powder (s07)
~1/3 the sodium of table salt gram for gram; swapping some salt cuts sodium 'noticeably', keeps flavor (s08) - no % reduction
'Even water' in absurd amounts; 'about as dangerous as the tomato on your pizza' (s09)
Navigation text: 'PART n/3', 'PART 2 →', 'PART 3 →', part titles from script.py PARTS
forbidden: Any number, %, chart value, axis label, study count, dose or date not listed above (no '1909', no mg/kg, no 'n=', no per-food glutamate amounts).
Health claims beyond the script ('heart healthy', 'cures', 'zero side effects').
Real logos, mastheads, seals, networks, platforms or brands - plain text names only; invented channel names.
Real or recognisable people; the cold-open heads are fictional composites. The 1968 letter writer and the 1969 scientist are never named or drawn.
Gore: no needle entering an animal, no dead mice, no lesion imagery.
Burned-in captions are not 'on-screen text': keyword text must stay short and must not be a second subtitle track.
guardrails.dramatization: Every frame with a cold-open talking head (s01.01-06, s09.01, s09.04-06) carries the DRAMATIZATION tag (lower-third + TOP pill). Role labels are generic: TALK SHOW HOST, DAYTIME TV DOCTOR, CELEBRITY CHEF, WELLNESS INFLUENCER, YOUR AUNT, ON SOCIAL MEDIA.
sensitive_1960s_section: Applies to s01.04, s06 (whole scene, esp. s06.06, s06.09, s06.16-19) and s09.05.
No caricatured Asian people; in s06 no restaurant staff or diners are drawn at all - paper, type, newsprint and objects only (matches director's rules).
No 'oriental' signifiers: no wonton/chop-suey fonts, pagodas, lanterns, dragons, gongs, conical hats, chopsticks as decoration. Takeout = plain white carton.
Prejudice shown as cold tags / a ringing bell put ON the food, never as a trait of people; 'foreign'/'suspicious' in quotes.
Headline shown verbatim, hyphenated, in quotation marks, as a historical artifact being critiqued - never a joke or brand.
